strengths: Novel latent-space formulation for privacy preservation that is practical for large video foundation models, avoiding expensive retraining required by pixel-level methods

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across five diverse downstream tasks (action recognition on 3 datasets, temporal action detection, anomaly detection) demonstrating strong generalization to unseen tasks
Lightweight and scalable solution with 88.7% fewer trainable parameters than prior work, enabling easy application to frozen encoders and large pretrained models
Well-designed training framework with three complementary objectives, validated through extensive ablation studies showing necessity of each component
Impressive data efficiency: effective generalization from small datasets like HMDB51 with minimal performance degradation on unseen tasks
First systematic evaluation and mitigation of gender bias in video action recognition models, showing 39-42% bias reduction
Clear presentation with strong motivation, well-structured methodology, and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited formal privacy analysis: no differential privacy bounds or theoretical privacy guarantees; relies on single metric (cMAP on VISPR); no quantitative verification that mutual information is minimized; threat model limited to linear classifiers

Insufficient justification for core technical choices: NT-Xent loss as privacy objective lacks rigorous justification beyond intuition; simple L2 consistency loss (Eq. 6) not ablated against alternatives; connection between contrastive similarity and information destruction not formally established
Hyperparameter sensitivity not thoroughly explored: multiple critical parameters (ωLC, ωT, ωB) with ablations only for ωLC; no principled guidance for selecting hyperparameters for new applications

Gender bias evaluation limitations: binary gender formulation acknowledged as non-inclusive but not addressed; limited to gender bias without evaluating other demographics (age, race); artificial bias injection (95-5%) may not reflect realistic distributions; unclear whether improvements stem from privacy or feature distortion

Temporal attribute vulnerability: Table 6 reveals dramatic performance gaps without latent consistency (26.67% vs 69.73%), indicating complementary failure modes and suggesting method may not robustly protect all sensitive information

Limited baseline comparisons: main comparisons against SPAct and TeD-SPAD from same research group; no comparison with orthogonal privacy approaches (federated learning, differential privacy, secure computation)
Reproducibility concerns: project page URL not provided; code availability not explicitly mentioned; some implementation details potentially unclear for reproduction

Privacy evaluation limited to linear classifiers on a small set of attributes; no analysis of information theoretically what remains in anonymized features; no evaluation against non-linear privacy attacks

strengths: Novel and practical problem formulation: latent-space anonymization for video foundation models addresses a timely challenge with clear real-world applicability and advantages over pixel-level methods

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: extensive experiments across 5+ downstream tasks, multiple datasets (Kinetics400, UCF101, HMDB51, THUMOS14, UCF-Crime), and different architectures (I3D, VideoMAE, VJEPA, InternVideo), with thorough ablations
Strong empirical results: achieves 35% reduction in privacy leakage while maintaining near-baseline utility (within 1-2%), demonstrating effective privacy-utility tradeoff across diverse tasks

Practical and efficient design: lightweight AAM with 88.7% fewer parameters than prior methods, no retraining required, 3.5x faster training, works across frozen models and scales to large foundation models

Well-designed training framework: three complementary objectives (clip-level self-supervised privacy, co-training utility, latent consistency) with latent consistency loss being particularly clever for preventing overfitting to proxy tasks

Novel contribution on fairness: first work to introduce evaluation protocols for gender bias in video action recognition, demonstrating that privacy preservation also mitigates gender bias (39.5-42.3% gap reduction)
Robustness analysis: evaluates black-box and white-box attacks, reconstruction attacks, temporal attributes (gait), and generalizes to unseen tasks with data efficiency on small datasets
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: adapts NT-Xent loss from prior work (Dave et al. 2022b, Fioresi et al. 2023) to latent space; main contribution is L2 consistency regularizer, which while effective, represents incremental technical advance

Informal privacy model: lacks formal privacy definitions (e.g., differential privacy, information-theoretic bounds), evaluates only against supervised attribute classifiers, assumes adversary has both features and labels, making threat model limited and unclear

White-box vulnerability: privacy cMAP of 73.7% under white-box attacks vs. 58.8% under black-box (Table 8) represents significant gap; limited discussion of defenses or mitigation strategies for high-security scenarios

Weak theoretical justification: lacks rigorous explanation for why minimizing static-clip mutual information removes privacy-sensitive attributes like gender; missing analysis of what spatial vs. temporal information is preserved/removed

Restricted applicability: only works for global-embedding tasks, cannot handle dense predictions (segmentation, captioning); binary gender formulation limits fairness claims despite acknowledgment; scope narrower than claimed in abstract

Hyperparameter sensitivity: multiple hyperparameters (ωLC=100, ωT, ωB) with non-monotonic sensitivity; limited guidance for practitioners; Table 4 suggests task-specific tuning needed despite claims of generalizability

Limited unseen task evaluation: only 3 proxy tasks in training; 'unseen' tasks mostly evaluated via Table 5 ablation; single-architecture evaluation for truly new tasks (retrieval, Table 13); no evaluation on other common video tasks

Incomplete statistical rigor: no error bars, standard deviations, or significance testing reported; unclear if results are single runs or averaged; reproducibility details regarding seeds and multiple runs missing
